intro: Two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, and Kadane's algorithm are the four workhorse techniques for turning an O(n^2) or O(n^3) brute-force scan over an array or string into an O(n) or O(n log n) pass. They share a common theme: instead of recomputing information about a range from scratch every time the range changes, each technique maintains a running summary (a pointer position, a window's aggregate, a running sum, a running best) and updates it incrementally as the range slides or grows. Mastering when each invariant applies -- and, just as importantly, recognizing when it breaks (e.g. negative numbers breaking sliding-window monotonicity) and you need to fall back to prefix sums plus a hash map or monotonic deque -- is what separates easy-tier from hard-tier array problems.

subtopics.name: Two Pointers
subtopics.theory:
The two-pointer technique maintains two (or more) indices into a sequence and advances them according to a rule that guarantees each pointer only ever moves forward (or at least never revisits work already done). The key structural requirement is monotonicity: as one pointer advances, some measured quantity (a sum, a count, a difference) must change in a predictable, one-directional way, so that you never need to re-examine a position once you have moved past it. This is what lets an algorithm that looks like it should be O(n^2) (for every left endpoint, scan forward until some condition breaks) collapse to O(n): each pointer traverses the array once, so total pointer movement is bounded by O(n) even though there are two nested-looking loops.

The classic setups are: (1) opposite-direction pointers starting at both ends of a sorted array and moving inward, used for problems like pair-sum-to-target, 3Sum, and container/trapping-water problems, where sortedness gives you the monotonic guarantee that lets you decide deterministically which pointer to move; and (2) same-direction pointers (often called the 'fast/slow' or 'read/write' pattern) used for in-place partitioning, de-duplication, and merging. A subtler but very powerful variant fixes one pointer and lets the other pointer only ever move forward as the fixed pointer advances, which is the basis of the sliding window technique covered next -- sliding window is really just two pointers with the extra constraint that the region between them defines a contiguous window whose aggregate you maintain incrementally.

Two pointers is not just for searching -- it composes well with combinatorial counting. A common hard-problem pattern is: sort the array, then for each right pointer position find (via a monotonically advancing left pointer) the maximal valid window, and instead of enumerating pairs one by one, count how many subsequences/subsets that window supports using combinatorics (nCr). This turns an O(n^2) pair-counting problem into O(n log n) (dominated by the sort).

A critical failure mode to internalize: two pointers relies on monotonicity of the underlying quantity as a pointer moves. The moment negative numbers (or any non-monotonic element) enter the picture for a sum-based window, advancing/shrinking the window no longer has a well-defined 'always helps' or 'always hurts' direction, and two pointers silently gives wrong answers rather than failing loudly -- that is exactly when you should reach for prefix sums with a hash map instead.
subtopics.recognition: Look for problems on a sorted (or sortable) array/string asking about pairs, triplets, or windows defined by a monotonic condition (sum, difference, or count that only increases/decreases as a pointer moves) -- especially phrasings like 'find a pair/triplet with sum X', 'is the array a palindrome', or 'maximum area between two indices'.
subtopics.complexity: Typically O(n log n) if sorting is required first, otherwise O(n); O(1) extra space beyond the pointers and, if needed, an output buffer.

examples.title: Bounded-Range Subsequences (Close Tuples, hard version)
examples.problem: You are given n integers a_1, ..., a_n and integers m and k. Count the number of subsequences (chosen by index, order in the original array does not matter for the value of the subsequence) of size exactly m such that the difference between the maximum and minimum element of the chosen subsequence is at most k. Two subsequences are different if the sets of chosen indices differ. Print the answer modulo 998244353. Constraints: 1 <= m <= n <= 2*10^5, 0 <= k <= 10^9, 0 <= a_i <= 10^9.
examples.approach: Because we are counting subsets of indices and the max-minus-min condition only depends on the multiset of chosen values (not their original positions), we can sort the array first: the number of size-m index-subsets of the original array satisfying the property equals the number of size-m index-subsets of the sorted array satisfying it, since sorting is just a relabeling. Once sorted, fix the subsequence's maximum element to be a[i] (the element at the largest chosen index i in the sorted order). Every earlier element a[j] with a[i]-a[j] <= k is a legal partner. Because the array is sorted, the condition a[i]-a[j] <= k is monotonic in j: as i increases, the smallest valid j (call it left) only moves right, never left. So we sweep i left-to-right and advance a single 'left' pointer forward whenever a[i]-a[left] > k -- classic two pointers, O(n) total pointer movement. For each i, the number of usable earlier elements is cnt = i - left, and we must choose m-1 of them to accompany a[i] as the fixed maximum, contributing C(cnt, m-1) subsequences (choosing a[i] itself fixes one slot). Summing C(cnt, m-1) over all i gives the total count, with no double-counting because each subsequence is counted exactly once, at the index of its maximum element in sorted order. Precomputing factorials and inverse factorials mod p makes each nCr O(1).

examples.title: 3Sum: Unique Zero-Sum Triplets
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums, find all unique triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] (i, j, k distinct indices) such that nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0. Print each distinct triplet's values in non-decreasing order, one triplet per line, with the triplets themselves ordered by their first element then second element (ties broken naturally by the scanning order described below). Do not print the same value-triplet twice even if it arises from multiple index choices.
examples.approach: Sort the array first. Fix the smallest element of the triplet at index i by iterating i from 0 to n-3, skipping any i where a[i] equals the previous element (to avoid emitting a duplicate triplet). For the remaining subarray a[i+1..n-1], we need a pair summing to -a[i]: since that subarray is sorted, use opposite-direction two pointers left = i+1 and right = n-1. If a[i]+a[left]+a[right] is too small, the only way to increase the sum is to move left rightward (monotonicity: increasing left only increases the value picked, since the array is sorted); if too large, move right leftward. When the sum equals zero, record the triplet, then advance both pointers past any run of equal values (again to avoid duplicate output). This is the two-pointer invariant in its purest form: because the array is sorted, moving a pointer always changes the sum in a known direction, so we never need to backtrack.

examples.title: Trapping Rain Water
examples.problem: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, 0 <= height[i] <= 10^5.
examples.approach: The water trapped above position i equals min(maxHeightToLeft(i), maxHeightToRight(i)) - height[i]. Computing both max-to-left and max-to-right arrays with prefix/suffix scans works in O(n) time and O(n) space, but two pointers gets it down to O(1) extra space using the following invariant: maintain pointers left and right at the two ends and running maxima leftMax, rightMax. At each step, whichever side currently has the smaller height tells you the water level there with certainty -- if height[left] <= height[right], then even though we don't yet know the true maximum on the right side, we know it is at least height[right] >= height[left], so the water trapped at 'left' is fully determined by leftMax (the true bottleneck must be on the left since the right side already has a wall at least as tall as anything blocking us from the left). This lets us resolve position 'left' immediately and advance the left pointer inward, and symmetrically for the right side. Each position is resolved exactly once as one of the two pointers passes it, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.

subtopics.name: Sliding Window
subtopics.theory:
Sliding window is the specialization of two pointers to problems about contiguous ranges (subarrays or substrings) where you maintain some aggregate statistic of the current window (a sum, a frequency table, a count of distinct elements, a count of characters still needed) and update that aggregate incrementally as the window's boundaries move, rather than recomputing it from scratch. There are two flavors: fixed-size windows, where both endpoints move together by one step each iteration (e.g. 'maximum in every window of size k'), and variable-size windows, where the right endpoint always advances but the left endpoint only advances when some validity condition is violated (e.g. 'smallest window containing all of these characters').

The correctness argument for variable-size sliding window rests on a monotonicity property: as the window grows (right pointer advances), the tracked condition moves in one direction (e.g. adding more of a non-negative-sum array only increases the sum; adding more characters only increases or maintains the count of 'still needed' characters), and as the window shrinks (left pointer advances) it moves in the opposite direction. Because both endpoints are non-decreasing over the whole scan, the total work across the whole algorithm is O(n) even though it looks like a nested loop -- this is the amortized/two-pointer argument again, just applied to a window's aggregate instead of two independent search pointers.

When the aggregate you need is not a simple running sum/count but something like 'the maximum element currently in the window', a plain running variable cannot be updated in O(1) when elements leave the window from the left (you'd have to rescan). The standard fix is a monotonic deque: keep indices in the deque in an order such that their values are monotonic (decreasing for a max-window, increasing for a min-window), popping from the back whenever a new incoming element would make an existing back-of-deque element useless (it's smaller and will leave the window no later than the new element), and popping from the front when the front index falls outside the current window. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so this maintains window max/min in amortized O(1) per step.

A very useful meta-trick when a problem asks for 'exactly K' of something (exactly K distinct values, exactly K odd numbers, etc.) is to solve the easier 'at most K' sliding-window version twice and subtract: countExactly(K) = countAtMost(K) - countAtMost(K-1). 'At most' conditions are monotonic in the window (shrinking the window can only decrease the count of distinct values, say), which is exactly the property plain sliding window needs, whereas 'exactly K' by itself is not monotonic and cannot be solved directly by a single sliding window.
subtopics.recognition: Look for 'contiguous subarray/substring' problems asking for a max/min/count over windows of a given size, or the smallest/largest window satisfying some containment or frequency condition -- especially when all values involved are non-negative (so growing the window is 'monotonically worse or better').
subtopics.complexity: O(n) or O(n log n) if a heap is used instead of a monotonic deque; O(k) or O(alphabet size) extra space for the window's aggregate structure.

examples.title: Sliding Window Maximum
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums of size n and an integer k, there is a sliding window of size k which moves from the very left of the array to the very right, one position at a time. Return the maximum value in the window at each position it stops at (there are n-k+1 such positions). Constraints: 1 <= k <= n <= 10^5.
examples.approach: Maintain a deque of indices whose corresponding values are strictly decreasing from front to back. For each new index i: first pop from the back while the value at the back index is <= nums[i], since those back elements can never be the maximum again (nums[i] is at least as large and will outlive them in the window); push i onto the back. Then pop from the front if the front index has fallen out of the current window (index <= i - k). The front of the deque is now always the index of the maximum value within the current window, because it's the largest remaining value and everything larger that could have competed with it has already left the window or was popped for being smaller than something still present. Once i >= k-1 the window is fully formed and we record the front's value as this window's maximum. Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once, giving O(n) total time.

examples.title: Minimum Window Substring
examples.problem: Given two strings s and t of lengths n and m, return the minimum-length contiguous substring of s that contains every character of t, including duplicates (i.e. for each character, the substring must contain at least as many occurrences as t does). If no such substring exists, print an empty line. Constraints: 1 <= m <= n <= 10^5, both strings consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters.
examples.approach: This is the canonical variable-size sliding window: expand the right endpoint one character at a time, updating a frequency map of the current window and a counter 'formed' tracking how many distinct required characters currently meet their required count. Once formed equals the number of distinct characters in t, the window is valid, and we greedily shrink from the left as far as possible while it stays valid, recording the shortest valid window seen. Shrinking is safe/correct because removing characters from the left can only ever reduce coverage (monotonic: a valid window that becomes invalid after removing one more character from the left is exactly the boundary we want to record right before it breaks). Because the right pointer only moves forward n times and the left pointer only moves forward at most n times total across the whole run, the algorithm is O(n + m) despite the nested while loop.

examples.title: Subarrays with Exactly K Different Integers
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums of length n and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays that contain exactly k different (distinct) integer values. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^4, 1 <= k <= n, 1 <= nums[i] <= n.
examples.approach: 'Exactly k distinct' is not directly monotonic under window growth/shrink in the way plain sliding window needs, but 'at most k distinct' is: as you shrink the window from the left, the number of distinct values can only stay the same or decrease. So define atMost(X) = number of subarrays with at most X distinct values, computed with a standard variable-size sliding window (expand right, track distinct count via a frequency map, shrink left whenever distinct count exceeds X; every window ending at 'right' that is currently valid contributes (right-left+1) new subarrays, since every subarray ending at 'right' with left endpoint in [left, right] is valid). Then exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1), because every subarray with at most k distinct values either has at most k-1 distinct values or has exactly k -- subtracting removes precisely the 'k-1 or fewer' subarrays, leaving only those with exactly k. This 'atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)' trick generalizes to many 'exactly K' window-counting problems.

subtopics.name: Prefix Sums
subtopics.theory:
A prefix sum array P, where P[0] = 0 and P[i] = a[0] + a[1] + ... + a[i-1], lets you answer 'what is the sum of the subarray a[l..r]?' in O(1) time as P[r+1] - P[l], after O(n) preprocessing. This is the single most important trick for turning repeated range-sum queries (or the search for a range with a target sum) from O(n) per query into O(1) per query. The invariant is trivial to maintain (a single running total as you scan left to right), but its consequences are powerful: any problem phrased in terms of 'sum of some contiguous range' can be re-expressed as a problem about a difference of two values in the prefix array, which converts a 2D search space (all pairs l, r) into effectively a 1D one.

The key unlock this gives you over two pointers/sliding window is handling negative numbers correctly. Sliding window relies on the property that growing a window changes the tracked sum in a known, monotonic direction; with negative elements present, growing the window could increase or decrease the sum, so you can no longer decide which pointer to move. Prefix sums sidestep this entirely: 'find a subarray with sum exactly x' becomes 'find two prefix indices i < j with P[j] - P[i] = x', i.e. 'for each j, has P[j] - x been seen before as some earlier P[i]?' -- which is answered by scanning once and looking up P[j] - x in a hash map of prefix sums seen so far, incrementing the map with P[j] afterward. This works regardless of the sign of any element, at the cost of O(n) extra space for the hash map (versus O(1) for plain sliding window when it applies).

Prefix sums generalize cleanly to two dimensions: a 2D prefix sum table lets you compute the sum of any axis-aligned submatrix in O(1) after O(R*C) preprocessing, using inclusion-exclusion (sum = P[r2+1][c2+1] - P[r1][c2+1] - P[r2+1][c1] + P[r1][c1]). This is the standard way to reduce 'submatrix sum' problems to repeated 1D 'subarray sum' problems: fix a pair of column boundaries, compute the resulting 1D array of row-range sums using the 2D prefix table, and run the 1D prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique on that array.

Prefix sums also combine with a monotonic deque when a problem asks for something like the shortest (or otherwise optimal) subarray meeting a sum threshold, in the presence of negative numbers where a simple non-negative-only sliding window (which would work if all values were non-negative) breaks down. There, you keep prefix indices in a deque ordered by increasing prefix value; because a later, smaller prefix value always makes a better (or equal) starting point than an earlier, larger one, you can safely discard dominated candidates, giving an O(n) sweep even though sums are not monotonic.
subtopics.recognition: Look for 'count/find a subarray with sum exactly/at least X' where the array can contain negative or zero elements (ruling out plain sliding window), or any problem asking for repeated range-sum queries over a fixed array/matrix.
subtopics.complexity: O(n) preprocessing plus O(1) per range-sum query; O(n) or O(n) extra space for the prefix array and any hash map/deque used alongside it. 2D prefix sums cost O(R*C) preprocessing.

examples.title: Subarray Sums II (allows negatives)
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers (which may be negative, zero, or positive) and a target integer x, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals exactly x. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, -10^9 <= a_i, x <= 10^9.
examples.approach: Because elements can be negative, growing or shrinking a sliding window does not change the window sum monotonically, so plain two pointers cannot be used here (unlike the easier variant of this problem restricted to non-negative values). Instead, compute the running prefix sum P as you scan left to right, and maintain a hash map from prefix-sum-value to how many times it has occurred so far (initialized with P=0 occurring once, representing the empty prefix before index 0). At each position, a subarray ending here with sum x exists for every earlier prefix value equal to (current prefix - x); look that up in the map and add its count to the answer, then record the current prefix value in the map. This is O(n) time with O(n) hash-map space, and correctly handles negative numbers because it never relies on the sum changing monotonically -- it only relies on prefix-sum equality.

examples.title: Number of Submatrices That Sum to Target
examples.problem: Given an R x C integer matrix and an integer target, return the number of non-empty submatrices (axis-aligned, contiguous ranges of rows and columns) whose element sum equals target. Constraints: 1 <= R, C <= 100, -1000 <= matrix[i][j] <= 1000, -10^8 <= target <= 10^8.
examples.approach: Build a 2D prefix-sum table P where P[i][j] is the sum of the submatrix from (0,0) to (i-1,j-1), so any submatrix sum can be read off in O(1) via inclusion-exclusion. Then reduce the 2D problem to O(C^2) instances of the 1D 'count subarrays summing to target' problem: fix a pair of column boundaries (c1, c2) with c1 <= c2, and for each row r compute the sum of that row restricted to columns [c1, c2] using the 2D prefix table in O(1); this produces a 1D array of length R. Run prefix sums plus a hash map (exactly as in the previous example) on that 1D array to count how many row-ranges sum to target for this fixed column pair, and add that to the running answer. Trying every pair of column boundaries costs O(C^2), and each column pair does O(R) work, for a total of O(R * C^2), which is efficient enough given R, C <= 100.

examples.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums (which may contain negative numbers) of length n and an integer k, return the length of the shortest, non-empty, contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k. If no such subarray exists, return -1. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^5, -10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5, 1 <= k <= 10^9.
examples.approach: Because negatives are allowed, a plain sliding window (valid only when growing a window is guaranteed to help, i.e. all-non-negative arrays) does not work. Instead, build the prefix sum array P[0..n]. A subarray (i, j] with sum >= k corresponds to P[j] - P[i] >= k for some i < j; we want to minimize j - i. Maintain a deque of candidate left-endpoints i with the invariant that P over the deque is strictly increasing from front to back. For each new j (scanning P left to right): first, while the front of the deque gives P[j] - P[front] >= k, that candidate satisfies the sum condition -- record j - front as a candidate answer and pop it from the front, since any larger j' > j will only give an equal-or-worse (larger) length using that same front, so it can never be optimal again once beaten by this j. Second, before pushing j itself as a future left endpoint, pop from the back any index whose prefix value is >= P[j], because such an index is strictly dominated by j (j is a later, and at-least-as-low, starting point, so it will always produce an equal-or-shorter valid subarray whenever the dominated index would have worked). Each index enters and leaves the deque once, giving O(n) total time.

subtopics.name: Kadane's Algorithm
subtopics.theory:
Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in O(n) time using a single dynamic-programming pass. Define best(i) as the maximum sum of a subarray ending exactly at index i. The recurrence is best(i) = max(a[i], best(i-1) + a[i]): either the best subarray ending at i is just a[i] on its own (restart), or it extends the best subarray ending at i-1 by adding a[i]. The overall answer is max over all i of best(i). The crucial insight that makes this a genuine dynamic-programming/greedy hybrid rather than a brute-force check is that once best(i-1) is negative, it can never help any future subarray sum (adding a negative running total only drags down whatever comes next), so restarting from a[i] alone dominates. This lets you keep only a single rolling value ('cur') instead of the full best(i) array, giving O(1) space in addition to O(n) time -- a dramatic improvement over the naive O(n^2) (try every start) or O(n^3) (try every start and end, resumming each time) approaches.

Kadane's is best understood as a special, very efficient case of the general prefix-sum reformulation: the maximum subarray sum ending at j is P[j] - min(P[0..j-1]) where P is the prefix sum array. Kadane's algorithm computes this implicitly by tracking the running minimum prefix (equivalently, the running best partial sum) as it scans, without needing to materialize the full prefix array or search it explicitly. Seeing this connection is what unlocks the harder variants below: whenever a variant constrains which earlier prefix indices are eligible (e.g. only prefixes within a certain distance back), you can no longer just track a single running minimum -- you need a windowed-minimum structure (segment tree or monotonic deque) over the eligible prefix indices, which is exactly sliding-window-minimum applied to the prefix array.

Two very common hard variants build directly on the base algorithm. First, length-constrained maximum subarray sum (maximize sum subject to the subarray length falling in [minLen, maxLen]): here you compute prefix sums P and, for each right endpoint r, need the minimum P[j] over j in the valid window [r-maxLen, r-minLen] -- a sliding-window-minimum problem over the prefix array, solved with a monotonic deque in O(n) total, since as r increases the valid window of j slides forward monotonically. Second, maximum subarray sum in a circular array (the subarray may wrap past the end back to the start): the best circular-wrapping subarray is total sum minus the minimum-sum non-circular subarray (removing the smallest-sum contiguous 'hole' from the full circle leaves the best wraparound segment), so compute ordinary Kadane's max, and a mirrored Kadane's-for-minimum, and take max(ordinarKadaneMax, total - minSubarraySum) -- with the edge case that if every element is negative, the minimum subarray is the entire array, making the wrap candidate an invalid empty selection, so you must fall back to the plain (negative) Kadane's max in that case.
subtopics.recognition: Look for 'maximum (or minimum) sum contiguous subarray' phrasing, especially when a plain 'sum of all elements' or 'largest element' answer is clearly too simple to be the intended solution -- length bounds, circularity, or a two-dimensional (submatrix) version are the standard ways these problems get escalated to hard difficulty.
subtopics.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space for the base algorithm; O(n log n) or O(n) (with a monotonic deque) for length-constrained variants; O(n) time and space for the circular-array variant.

examples.title: Maximum Subarray Sum with Witness Indices
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers (which may be negative), find the maximum possible sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray. In addition to the sum, output the 0-indexed start and end indices of a subarray achieving that maximum sum, specifically the one produced by scanning left to right and, whenever the running sum would need to restart, restarting exactly at the current element (this makes the output deterministic). Print the sum, then the start index, then the end index, separated by spaces. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^5.
examples.approach: This is the base Kadane recurrence, best(i) = max(a[i], best(i-1) + a[i]), tracked with a single rolling variable 'cur' plus its current start index. Whenever cur would become negative after adding the previous element (i.e. cur < 0 before processing a[i]), it is strictly better to restart the running subarray at a[i] alone, since carrying forward a negative running sum can only hurt any future extension -- so we reset cur = a[i] and mark the new candidate start as i. Otherwise we extend by cur += a[i]. After each update we compare cur to the best sum seen so far and, if it improves, record the sum along with the current candidate's start and the current index as its end. This single left-to-right pass is O(n) time and O(1) extra space (beyond the input array).

examples.title: Maximum Subarray Sum with Length Bounds
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers (which may be negative) and two integers a and b with 1 <= a <= b <= n, find the maximum possible sum of a contiguous subarray whose length L satisfies a <= L <= b. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, -10^9 <= values <= 10^9.
examples.approach: Plain Kadane's does not enforce any length constraint, so instead work with prefix sums P[0..n] (P[0]=0). The sum of a subarray ending at prefix index r (i.e. covering original indices [j, r-1]) with left prefix-boundary j is P[r] - P[j], and its length is r - j; we need a <= r-j <= b, i.e. j must lie in the window [r-b, r-a]. To maximize P[r] - P[j] for fixed r we want the minimum P[j] over that window -- a sliding-window-minimum problem on the prefix array. As r increases by 1, the window [r-b, r-a] slides forward by exactly 1 on both ends, so maintain a monotonic increasing deque of prefix indices: each step, add the newly-eligible index r-a to the deque (popping any back entries with a prefix value >= the new one, since they're now dominated), then pop any front entries that have fallen below the window's lower bound r-b. The front of the deque is always the minimum-prefix eligible index, so P[r] - P[front] is the best achievable sum ending at r, and we take the max of that quantity over all valid r.

examples.title: Maximum Circular Subarray Sum
examples.problem: Given a circular integer array nums of length n (meaning the subarray is allowed to wrap around past the last element back to the first), return the maximum possible sum of a non-empty contiguous (possibly wrapping) subarray. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 3*10^4, -3*10^4 <= nums[i] <= 3*10^4.
examples.approach: A subarray that does not wrap is just handled by ordinary Kadane's algorithm, giving maxSub. A subarray that does wrap around consists of a prefix of the array plus a suffix of the array, with some contiguous 'hole' in the middle excluded; its sum equals total - (sum of the excluded middle segment). To maximize the wrapped sum we therefore want to minimize the sum of the excluded middle segment, i.e. compute minSub, the minimum-sum non-empty contiguous subarray, using a mirrored Kadane's recurrence (curMin = min(a[i], curMin + a[i])). The best circular answer is then total - minSub, and the overall answer is max(maxSub, total - minSub). The one subtlety: if every element is negative, minSub equals the sum of the entire array, making total - minSub equal to 0, which corresponds to excluding everything -- an empty (invalid) selection. In that case the wrap candidate must be discarded and the answer is simply maxSub (which will correctly be the least-negative single element). This is handled by checking whether maxSub itself is negative before considering the wrap candidate.
